title: Why You Need To Bring More Humor To Your Classroom
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin makes the case that humor, while not mandatory, is one of the most underused tools in classroom management, and that a teacher merely needs to be open to it rather than naturally funny. Drawing on his own long career of using celebrity voices, costumes, and silly stories, he explains that humor works because students are an unusually forgiving and receptive audience who reward even small effort. He is careful to note that humor is a supplement to, not a substitute for, an actual classroom management system, and warns against overusing it. The article's core argument is built around three concrete benefits: humor widens the emotional gap between being part of the well-behaved class and being excluded from it, which makes consequences matter more; it makes a teacher more approachable and speeds up rapport-building; and it increases a teacher's influence, since students only take advice seriously from adults they like. He closes by framing the classroom as a limited-time, emotionally memorable experience worth making joyful.
points: You don't need to be naturally funny — merely being open to humor and picking your spots is enough to get its benefits.
Humor widens the emotional gap between being part of the well-behaved class and sitting in time-out, making consequences matter more to students.
Being funny makes a teacher more approachable, which speeds up rapport and lowers fear and shyness in students.
Students only take advice, encouragement, and correction seriously from teachers they like — humor builds the likability that creates real influence.
Humor supplements, but never substitutes for, an actual classroom management system; without that foundation it risks losing control of the class.
quotes: You see, students are primed to laugh. They’re the most receptive and forgiving audience in the world. It doesn’t take much and they’re so appreciative of the effort.

I’ve used celebrity voices, dressed and pretended I was someone else, tripped over chairs, answered phone calls with my shoe, sang opera while giving directions, danced ballet passing out assignments.
Humor helps widen the gap between the experience of being part of the class in good standing and sitting in time-out and not being allowed to take part.
When you tap into your own unique sense of humor, you become more approachable. Your likability soars and your students want to be around you and to get to know you better.

In this day and age especially, students won’t listen to your advice if they don’t like you. In fact, there must be admiration in order for them to take your advice, exhortations, and encouragement to heart.
Your classroom is an experience. It’s a moment in time that will stay with them for a lifetime. They’re only with you once, one year of their life, and then it’s over.
